As always, a nice update from Eric who remains bullish long term on the AI trade: 

"Remember Liberation Day? Remember the DeepSeek scare? Both caused panic. Both looked like the end of the AI trade at the time. Look where we are since then.

"The AI revolution isn’t collapsing. This is a speed bump."

He also notes that historically after large VIX spikes "Fear spikes. Then it fades. The market has a habit of rewarding those who don’t panic."

In that regard has he some stats on VIX spikes, but we also had an even more notable spike in the VVIX (the VIX of the VIX) which saw its biggest one-day percentage gain since February 2007 and its biggest point gain since Volmageddon in 2018.

We’ve had six cases since 2007 of the VIX rising at least 40% and the VVIX at least 30% on the same day. The S&P 500 was higher a month later in all six, by an average of 2.3%. At three months, though, only four of the six were higher, by an average of 2.3%. That’s no better than the S&P 500’s typical three-month gain since 2007, about 2.5%, which was higher 72% of the time, but is certainly not bear market material.

The outliers were October 10, 2018, and November 26, 2021. The October 2018 spike came as rising Treasury yields and the Fed’s hawkish push (it was a week before Powell's infamous “a long way from neutral" statement) hit tech stocks. It turned out to be the start of the fourth-quarter selloff, which took the S&P 500 down almost 20% by Christmas Eve, and the index was 6.8% lower three months later. 

The November 2021 spike was the Black Friday Omicron scare (followed days later by Powell saying it was time to retire the word “transitory” for inflation), although the S&P 500 would still peak in early January. Three months later it was down 4.8%, as Russia’s invasion of Ukraine deepened what became the 2022 bear market.

The common thread: in both misses the spike was an early warning of a macro shift, Fed tightening in particular, not a one-off scare or "speed bump" as Eric would say it is.

Much of this momentum is being fueled by the AI investment boom.

Orders for computers, servers, storage devices, and related equipment have surged +27% YoY, the largest annual increase since January 1997.

The AI infrastructure buildout is beyond massive.

🇫🇷 French Presidential Election 2027: 4 key takeaways from Polymarket & Kalshi ⬇️

🥇 Marine Le Pen remains the clear frontrunner (45–47%). Her legal path to running in 2027 has reopened following her appeal ruling while the fragmentation of the political centre continues to work in her favour. The National Rally also maintains a strong electoral base with recent polls putting her above 30% in first-round voting intentions.

🥈 David Lisnard climbs into second place (15%). The mayor of Cannes is gaining visibility as a pro-business, economically liberal alternative to the traditional centre-right. His recent surge on social media has helped attract attention, although his prediction-market momentum remains far stronger than his demonstrated support in conventional polling.

🥉 Jean-Luc Mélenchon remains firmly in contention (14%). Despite his polarizing image, he benefits from a loyal electoral base and the fragmentation of the French left. His chances of reaching the second round remain credible although his high rejection ratings could make winning a runoff significantly harder.

📉 Édouard Philippe continues to collapse (8.6–10%). Once considered the natural successor to Macron, he is struggling to distance himself from the president's unpopular legacy. Competition with Gabriel Attal, fragmentation of the centrist electorate and a campaign struggling to generate enthusiasm have pushed his market odds sharply lower.

➡️ Christine Lagarde is emerging as a wildcard (6–7%). Her announcement that she will leave the ECB early in February 2027 has triggered speculation about a potential presidential bid. With her international credibility and economic expertise, she could appeal to a centre-right electorate looking for an alternative. However, she has previously ruled out running, and no concrete campaign preparations have emerged.

*Bottom line: Prediction markets are pricing in a fragmented political centre with Le Pen benefiting from the absence of a convincing challenger. However, it is worth noting that these figures reflect betting-market probabilities, not voting intention polls.

tweets.text:
Thanks for engaging, @bchesky. I don’t presume you could never offer a price-match guarantee. You could, and so could Booking, Expedia and every other OTA which is part of my point. If agents check every major OTA by default, discovery matters less and more of the decision comes down to a price comparison at the last step. A price match may well keep the booking on Airbnb, but it does so by moving some of the surplus to the guest and, over time, to whoever owns the agent. I’m not arguing that agents cut Airbnb out, or that Airbnb or Booking go to zero. I’m pointing out that this could lower Airbnb’s economic profit and make it harder to keep compounding its earnings over the long term.

On apps, I actually didn’t design one, and I’m not suggesting people will want to. I spoke to Muse for about 30 seconds, it built the page, and I gave it some feedback over a couple of hours while walking with my son. That’s possible TODAY. In 3-5 years, I would expect the first version to need much less tweaking, so this may not remain just a hobbyist thing. And I agree I couldn’t design an app better than Airbnb’s.
